content: Iron deficiency has significantly increased, leading to a reduction in the effectiveness of anemia screening for detecting iron deficiency in the United States. The recognition of iron deficiency as a condition with broad and potentially serious negative effects has emphasized the importance of identifying individuals with iron deficiency, not just those with iron-deficiency anemia. The definition of anemia recommended in this report is based on hemoglobin (Hb) concentration or hematocrit (Hct) levels below the 5th percentile of a healthy reference population, adjusted for age, sex, and pregnancy stage (in pregnant women). This definition has been shown to correctly identify 37% of women of childbearing age and 25% of children aged 1–5 years who are iron deficient (sensitivity), while correctly classifying 93% of women of childbearing age and 92% of children aged 1–5 years as not having iron deficiency (specificity). Lowering the Hb or Hct cutoff values would reduce the number of false positives (individuals incorrectly identified as anemic due to causes other than iron deficiency) but would also result in missing more true positives (individuals with iron deficiency). The distributions of Hb and Hct, and therefore the cutoff values for anemia, vary by age, sex, pregnancy status, and gestational age, as well as by altitude, smoking status, and race. In pregnant women, Hb and Hct levels decline during the first and second trimesters due to an expanding blood volume. Among pregnant women who do not take iron supplements, Hb and Hct levels remain low in the third trimester. However, in those with adequate iron intake, Hb and Hct levels gradually rise during the third trimester, approaching pre-pregnancy levels. Due to a lack of adequate U.S. data, anemia cutoff values are based on clinical studies of European women who took iron supplementation during pregnancy. A high Hb concentration or Hct level in the second or third trimester of pregnancy should not be interpreted as an indicator of desirable iron status. For example, women with a Hct of ≥43% at 26–30 weeks of gestation had more than a twofold increased risk of preterm delivery and a fourfold increased risk of delivering a child with fetal growth retardation compared to women with a Hct of 33%–36%. Long-term residence at high altitudes (≥3,000 feet) and cigarette smoking cause a generalized upward shift in Hb and Hct levels. If anemia screening cutoff values are not adjusted for these factors, the effectiveness of screening is reduced. Adjusting for these factors ensures that the positive predictive value of anemia screening is comparable between individuals living at sea level and those at high altitudes, as well as between smokers and non-smokers.
